performers: Vladimir de Pachmann, piano (his own Baldwin)
intro: Pachmann plays the D♭-major Nocturne on his own Baldwin piano at Hayes in June 1925. The critic reviewing the disc that December rejoices in its phrasing — and in the famous pianist’s silence between the notes.

sections.label: A · A solo tune over D♭
sections.mNote: The left hand begins alone before F starts the melody

sections.label: B · A duet in thirds
sections.mNote: B♭ in the bass changes the harmony to minor

sections.label: C · The opening melody returns
sections.mNote: F sings above D♭ again, marked dolce

sections.label: D · The duet reaches C♯ minor
sections.mNote: G♯ in the bass supports the crowded right-hand voices

sections.label: E · A third statement in D♭
sections.mNote: The opening tune returns before the long ornamental flourish

sections.label: F · D♭ holds beneath the coda
sections.mNote: Changing chords above a recurring D♭ bass

cues.title: The piano begins alone
cues.text: For one bar the left hand has the whole piano to itself, spreading D♭ major into groups of six semiquavers. Then F begins the melody. Chopin asks for a slow, sustained song above the uninterrupted accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 1–4, Lento sostenuto and dolce. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Two voices on one keyboard
cues.text: The right hand doubles its song in thirds as the bass moves to B♭. The new phrase is marked espressivo. Little rests and ornaments make the two voices catch their breath together.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: “What a fine builder”
cues.text: The critic signing K.K. in The Gramophone, December 1925, greets this record with relief: “he does not utter a word the whole time”. Then comes the praise: “What a fine builder he is!” Pachmann’s phrasing survives the critic’s complaints about the recorded piano.
cues.evidence: K.K., review of HMV DB 860, The Gramophone, December 1925, pp. 338–339. https://archive.org/stream/gramophone-1925-12/Gramophone%201925-12_djvu.txt

cues.title: His own Baldwin
cues.text: Pachmann brings his own Baldwin to the Hayes session on 26 June 1925. The new electrical recording captures enough of the piano to trouble the December reviewer: some notes sound splendid, others clang. The critic nevertheless praises the pianist’s spirit.
cues.evidence: Session date, place, piano and electrical process: https://archive.org/details/hmv-db860-chopin-nocturne-no8-op27no2-etudes-op25no3-waltz-no7-op64no2. Contemporary comments: The Gramophone, December 1925, pp. 338–339, https://archive.org/stream/gramophone-1925-12/Gramophone%201925-12_djvu.txt

cues.title: D♭ and the first tune
cues.text: A falling run brings back the low D♭ and the opening melody. The right hand starts its third statement with the same F. Before long, that tune flowers into a long cascade of small notes.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A bass that stays
cues.text: The bass settles on D♭. The chords above it keep changing while pairs of notes in the right hand descend, marked dolcissimo. The left hand’s semiquavers still sweep across the keyboard.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Sixths into the distance
cues.text: The right hand climbs in sixths, two ribbons of notes rising together. Dolcissimo e diminuendo: very sweetly and growing softer. After the climb, the last D♭-major chord sits quietly beneath a pause.
cues.evidence: Claude Debussy edition (1915), bars 75–77: rising sixths, dolcissimo e diminuendo, pianissimo and final fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=486
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
